    #22077. Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (914 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

    Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk.
    • Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.
    • According to recent reports, as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk. At least 9 hours, too, which was way more than I had been getting.

    Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.

    According to recent reports, as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew. The girl was my age, and we discussed the Camino ending and what our lives would be like once we returned home. She was studying to be an actress and wanted to do so for the passion of it and to help people, not for the money or to be famous. She held many side jobs as a way to pay for her education and dream, one of them being teaching theater to children in a church. She spoke of the importance of giving young people a spiritual outlet, in whatever way felt best to them.

    The conversation then turned to my job and coaching. After telling her I help people find holistic balance in their life, she curiously asked me:.

    “How do you find balance in your life?”.

    This started a beautiful conversation about how we each live our lives, the things we prioritize, and our outlook on happiness and peace. A girl I’d met only a few days prior suddenly felt so familiar.

    But then up ahead, I saw the brothers.

    I yelled to them, and they waited for me to approach. With hugs and excitement, we all decided to go to a local restaurant, A Garnacha, for traditional Galician pulpo (octopus).

    With three orders of pulpo in front of us, we dove into the tentacles with the toothpicks we were given as utensils. Not many words were stated as we devoured our plates. The boys asked if I liked it, and the best I could say was,.

    “No es mi favorita, pero me gusta.”.

    For the first time in the whole Camino, the three of us walked together. Of course the Italian brother walked ahead, but we were still in close proximity.

    The three of us dropped our packs at a pilgrim rest area, and ended up spending over an hour there.

    We sang for the pilgrims that passed.

    We laughed while we rested all together.

    My Argentinian brother and I were shocked by the fact that our Italian brother sat for that long. Having just bought his plane ticket home, he was feeling the weight of the Camino ending and wanted to slow down over the next few days.

    He compared it to the last piece of pizza, and how you want to savor every single bite.

    We were all savoring each moment together like it was the last piece of pizza.

    The last part of the walk we did independently. I came up to a stream with a beautiful stone bridge over top. I took the moment to stop and be still, watching the ripples of the water reflect on the bridge. I pulled acorns out of the cold water and made a game of throwing them at a rock.

    Sources indicate that simplicity. That’s what I love about this lifestyle, and something I will greatly miss.

    When I arrived in the town of Arzúa and made it to the municipal albergue, Xunta de Galicia Arzúa Pilgrims Hostel, I showered and collapsed on my bunk.

    In a recent development, my Italian brother came and got me once our Argentinian brother arrived, and we all walked to a restaurant in search of Galician barbecue. They were out of the barbecue we were looking for, so we ordered almost the entire menu instead.

    Homemade croquettes, pimientos de Padrón (peppers), mixed salad, raxo, and milanesa de pollo.

    There was not a crumb left. We got cheesecake and flan to top it off while the boys talked about the intersection of futbol and politics. I completely zoned out and started to see just how tired we all were.

    That became quite evident in the street as we walked to find gelato. There was so much giggling and play, especially because we were delusional with exhaustion. But at one point, I walked behind the two of them as they were carrying on and thought,.

    “I love these two so damn much.”.

    And with a generous cone of gelato before bed, we all crashed for our last big day.

    Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
    • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
    • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

    “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

    The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

    However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

    It has been revealed that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

    “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

    Vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

    The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

    Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

    Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

    According to recent reports, baia indicates the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

    The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

    On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no newly introduced soft snow had accumulated.

    The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

    Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

    In a recent development, the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

    #22073. Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
    • According to recent reports, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
    • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

    According to recent reports, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin said. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

    “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

    Sources indicate that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

    This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” remarked Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

    In a recent development, for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he remarked.

    There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

    In a recent development, if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

    The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

    Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

    With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

    Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson mentioned. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

    According to recent reports, thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” noted Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

    It has been revealed that that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

    Buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they remarked. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

    The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

    Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the significant cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

    Sources indicate that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

    In a recent development, ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

    Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

    With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

    Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

    It has been revealed that in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

    It has been revealed that “That is why it is important to consider all options and potential challenges before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

    Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

    It has been revealed that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they stated. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

    They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing promptly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles remarked. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

    In a recent development, sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

    In a recent development, the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

    Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
    • The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
    • Recent findings suggest that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

    The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

    Recent findings suggest that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

    The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

    “He was really lucky,” noted Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

    By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.
    • It has been revealed that grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m.
    • The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.

    It has been revealed that grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m. on Saturday, November 14, according to a social media upgrade. The hikers had lost their way amid heavy snow and treacherous trail conditions near the High Lonesome Trail, which sits near the Continental Divide Trail mile marker 1,340.

    The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.

    Recent findings suggest that an initial response crew traveled up Rollins Pass Road on ATVs before continuing on foot deeper into the backcountry. Upon locating the trio, rescuers found them cold and exhausted and immediately provided warming gear, food, and support.

    Rather than waiting until sunrise, field leaders determined that keeping the hikers exposed at 11,600 feet in worsening conditions posed too great a danger. A second team was deployed to help walk the group out in the dark.

    According to recent reports, rescuers hike into the night. Photo via GCSAR.

    Sources indicate that rescuers and hikers reached the ATVs by 3:10 a.m. on Sunday, and all personnel cleared the field by 4:18 a.m.

    Backcountry Conditions and Safety Reminders.

    In their report, GCSAR notes that full winter conditions have already arrived at upper elevations, bringing deep snow, high winds, freezing temperatures, and rapidly shifting weather that can easily obscure trails above treeline.

    Officials advise anyone venturing into the mountains to pack proper winter layers and carry the ten essentials.

    GCSAR is staffed entirely by unpaid volunteers. The organization never bills rescue subjects and funds its gear, training, and rescue operations through public donations.

    Featured image: Grand County Search and Rescue.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (429 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
    • As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
    • Sources indicate that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

    As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

    Sources indicate that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

    In a recent development, hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

    Sources indicate that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

    Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed plan.

    Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

    Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

    It has been revealed that at the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

    #22062. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1694 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
    • In a recent development, gribbin introduced his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
    • The journey has not gone according to plan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

    In a recent development, gribbin introduced his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

    The journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

    While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

    How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

    Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid prepares. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

    But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

    How much has the weather affected your progress?

    Industry observers note that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

    Industry observers note that for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

    Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

    Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

    Sources indicate that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

    It has been revealed that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line reveals the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

    What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

    Recent findings suggest that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

    Recent findings suggest that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with upcoming designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

    Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

    Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

    It has been revealed that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

    What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

    Recent findings suggest that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

    Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

    Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

    Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

    Recent findings suggest that the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

    Sources indicate that I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

    It has been revealed that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

    We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

    There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

    How did you first get into the sport?

    According to recent reports, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

    Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

    According to recent reports, university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

    Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

    In a recent development, the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

    The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

    I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

    You can follow the expedition here.

    Industry News: No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
    • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
    • In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is rapidly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

    “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

    In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

    On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

    It has been revealed that once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

    On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

    It has been revealed that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

    #22057. Latest Update: Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2909 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry.
    • Recent findings suggest that it was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic.
    • According to recent reports, right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry. I wanted to get all packed up and then go in the hot tub first thing! That sounded like a wonderful way to start off the day. Last night I managed to coordinate a ride out of town with a few other hikers. The same kind man, Al, who we had breakfast with the other morning offered to drive a group back to the trailhead. About 5-6 hikers are getting back on trail at a road about 38 miles further south than where we’re getting back on trail. Al’s wife actually drove all of those hikers back to trail. Then Al was going to pick up Woods, Strix, and Leaf before coming to pick up Slide and myself around 9AM. That gave us plenty of time to go in the hot tub, shower, and have a little breakfast before hitting the trail.

    Recent findings suggest that it was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic. Slide and I soaked in there and then I took a final shower before we would be dirty hikers once more. The last couple of days off have been really nice. I needed the time to get some work done, and the trail needed some time to soak up all of the rain. I figure it we will still be dealing with the impacts of the storm for a little while, but hopefully it will be nothing in comparison to what it would have been like yesterday and the day before. After my shower I had a piece of pizza leftover from last night. Then I packed up the rest of my things and got ready to hit the road. We had talked about maybe walking down the road to the empanada place for breakfast. I absolutely love empanadas! But they didn’t open until 9AM and I didn’t want to make anyone wait for us, so we decided against it.

    According to recent reports, right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up. We loaded everything into Al’s truck and talked with everyone as we got ready to go. Strix has been dealing with some foot pain and is going to get dropped off right down the street to try and hitch into the larger town of Payson. Woods and Leaf are going to continue south on the trail just like us but will go into town sometime tomorrow from the highway crossing in 38 miles. That way they can hopefully link back up with Strix, and all continue on together from there. Slide and I are going to continue another 71 miles hopefully in the next 3 days and will head into the town of Payson in the evening. That will help to break up the next section of trail a little bit better so that we don’t have to carry as much food.

    A bridge that the trail crossed over in the early evening.

    It has been revealed that the ride to the trailhead took about 30 minutes but we got there eventually. It was so incredibly nice of Al to offer us a ride. And he made sure that we all had his phone number in case anyone needed some help over the next couple of days. That was really sweet of him. Then we were back on trail once more! It feels really good to be back at it after another double zero to avoid bad weather here in Arizona. We have now taken 5 zero days in the 17 days that we have been hiking the trail, which sounds absolutely crazy. It is in stark contrast to the way that Slide and I both hiked last year on our CYTC hikes. But we have the time to do it and hiking in that weather would have been really miserable. If not seriously dangerous. There are a couple different river crossings that we will have to go through tomorrow and the next day which would have hazardous or even impassable during the heavy rain. I’m curious to see how deep they will be only a couple of days after the rain has passed.

    Almost immediately when we began hiking south, we encountered patches of mud and areas where the trail was almost completely flooded. For the first couple of miles, we managed to navigate around the wetter sections while still keeping our feet dry. But that didn’t last long. Eventually there were areas where the trail was under about 4-5 inches of water consistently, and there was no good way around it. I was pretty happy though that the trail was wetter than it was muddy. Areas like this will often get a thick mud that sticks to your shoes and cakes on heavily. Walking in mud like that for miles can make your ankles and feet incredibly sore just from the weight of the mud alone. Slipping and sliding in mud can also make my hips and knees hurt, depending on how bad the mud is. At least the trail today was much more wet than it was muddy.

    A happy little mushroom just off the trail. All of the plants have been loving this rain.

    Sources indicate that when we were about 5 miles into the day the trail crossed over a dirt parking lot and trailhead. There were some large boulders surrounding the parking lot, so Slide and I decided to stop off there and enjoy a quick break. We’re only planning to hike around 20 miles today, so there is no need to rush. Woods and Leaf were somewhere behind us as well and it sounded nice to let everyone catch up. I was surprised how much mud and dirt was already coating my legs after only a handful of miles of hiking. The two of us hung out there for a while and then continued along. And right as we were leaving, I could see at least one of the girls approaching off in the distance. They weren’t far behind!

    Caked in mud and dirt, only 5 miles after leaving town.

    From there the trail continued through a forested area and we began to descend gradually. I could hear the loud roar of water off in the distance and began to wonder if we would be crossing the river that I could hear. Only a couple of miles after the trailhead where we had taken a break, we were now approaching a very large river. The trail did exactly what it always does when it requests you to cross a river. It descended all the way down until the trail disappeared and only the river laid before us. We had no choice but to cross it. The water looked deep and quite fast moving. I was not exactly eager to plunge into the freezing cold water. Slide on the other hand got right into the water and began to cross it. It’s always nice to gauge the water level on someone else before you also have to go through the water. We crossed right at the trail crossing and I could see the water rise to Slide’s upper thighs. He’s pretty tall so I knew that they water was going to be right up to the bottom of my shorts.

    A river that we had to cross this morning.

    I only had one trekking pole out which certainly wasn’t adequate for this crossing. The water was deep and very fast moving. With only one trekking pole I was not nearly stable enough. Plus, of course I was trying to record some videos of us crossing the water. I was glad that Slide was there on the other side. Otherwise, I would have probably had to pull my other trekking pole out to secure myself in that final stretch of the river crossing. But Slide just got back into the water and extended a hand to help me across that last little bit of river. Even though we had just stopped for a break less than an hour prior, we still decided to sit down there beside the river. I had a bunch of rocks in my shoes from crossing the river, and the girls likely weren’t far behind. They had each other so I wasn’t too worried about them. But they both are significantly shorter than Slide and me, so it seemed nice to wait around for them just in case.

    Slide helping Leaf across the river.

    According to recent reports, we sat there beside the river for a while, waiting to see if the girls arrived. And just as we were thinking about packing up and continuing along, I could see one of the girls crest over the hillside on the other side of the river. So, we decided to wait just a bit longer to let them get across. The first person to appear was Leaf, and we gave her some guidance for crossing the river. It was really deep though so Slide wound up just going over to her to help. He got into the river and met her about halfway through to help bring her to the other side. Then she joined us on the shore, and we sat and talked with her for a bit. In hindsight, I’m so glad that we waited for her. Because neither Slide nor I realized that the other hiker Wood’s had actually done a road walk earlier on in the day, which meant she was no longer heading in this direction. If we had continued on, then Leaf would have been stuck going through the fast-paced river alone. Knowing that no one else was anywhere close by behind her. I’m sure she would have been alright, but I was glad that we stuck around.

    The sign by the trailhead when we finally got off the dirt road and reconnected to the AZT.

    Sources indicate that before we headed out to continue along, we told Leaf that we were hoping to go around 20 miles. Hopefully she will go the same distance, and we can all camp together later this evening. She came out here to meet up with this group and hike with everyone, and now she’s basically alone. She’ll be able to link back up with everyone tomorrow, but it would be nice for her to not have to be alone on trail tonight. From there I wasn’t sure what to expect along the trail. That river crossing was a complete surprise to me, so who knows what is up ahead of us now. We wound up climbing for a while to get up and out of the area where we crossed the river. Once we got up top of the climb, the trail was completely dry and the trail turned in a double wide dirt road. Leaf had pointed out to us that the trail actually crossed over a road that we could continue along for a little while. It would wind up reconnecting with the AZT but might give a reprieve from any possible mud.

    The section of trail that we were hiking through just before dark was really beautiful.

    After a mile or two we arrived at that dirt road crossing and decided to continue along the road as well. It sounded like a nice way to get a handful of miles in without too much struggle. The road was really nice and quite dry which was delightful. We walked through a bunch of different logging operations alongside the road. Trees were piled high in preparation of them being transported somewhere. We even walked by a logging camp with a bunch of recreational vehicles. I’ve heard about guys camping out and living at these types of logging operations. There were generators running and we saw a couple of guys and a dog running around. I wonder if they will have to hold off on logging for a while after all of the rain.

    The sun beginning to set as we continued along the trail.

    The road had a lot of long hills for us to climb and descend, but eventually we began going downhill continuously for a while as we got closer to the AZT. Then we passed by another trailhead parking area and turned right to get back on the trail. The trail began descending rapidly once we reconnected to it. And we went right past a junction for some kind of mine that you can walk to right off the trail. Some hikers left comments indicating that it was a great place to hide out in bad weather. But we decided not to explore the side trail down to it today. We’ll be hiking until after dark this evening most likely and didn’t need to get sidetracked. We did stop off for another break though to put some more layers on as it was getting later. And we hoped that if we sat for a break then Leaf might catch up to us as well. Both of us really wanted her to catch up so that she wouldn’t have to camp alone tonight.

    Filtering water on the AZT with my platypus QuickDraw filter.

    The area that we were hiking through had numerous trailheads scattered throughout it, so we actually wound up seeing some day hikers not long after that. The trail also followed along a creek for a handful of miles toward the end of the day. It was great to have endless access to water if we needed it. We wound up stopping off and filling up on water sometime around 5PM, just so that we wouldn’t we wouldn’t have to worry about it for the rest of the night. And not long after that, the trail crossed over yet another trailhead. This one had a trail register as well, so I decided to leave a note for Leaf. I told her how much further we planned to go for the night in case she was close behind us and was hoping to camp together as well. Then we continued on with only a handful more miles to go for the day.

    Standing up from a final break before we continued on into the dark.

    Someone built this rock fort right next to the trail. I wonder how long it’s been there for.

    According to recent reports, the trail began to climb gradually after we left that trailhead. Which meant that we got wonderful views of the sunset as it began to light up the sky. It’s pretty typical for us to stop off and enjoy one final break before the sun goes down. Especially if we are hiking somewhere with great views of the sunset. This was too perfect to pass up. When we did get going again, we came across some cows that were hanging out right on the trail. I always feel bad for scaring the cows. We try to talk nicely to them when we go past, but most of the time you wind up scaring the cows either way.

    Industry observers note that the sunset this evening was incredible. It’s always my favorite time of the day!

    Eventually the sun went down, and we continued on in the dark for a little while longer. The area that we were hiking through did not seem like it was going to accommodate our need for a camp spot. So, when we finally did turn a corner and see a fairly flat area we decided to take advantage of it. There were some cow pies on the ground, and it wasn’t the best spot I’d ever seen, but it would work for tonight. The two of us got our tents set up and were hopeful that any minute now we would see Leaf’s headlamp coming around the corner. But that actually never happened. She must have stopped off for the night before the sun went down. Once my tent was set up, I got comfortable and had a little bit of dinner. Then did my stretching and a little editing in my tent before calling it a night.

    #22054. Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (342 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (342 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
    • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
    • It has been revealed that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

    A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

    It has been revealed that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

    In a recent development, eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

    It has been revealed that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He remarked climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

    The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

    The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

    Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

    Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

    Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

    This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

    With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

    Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a latest attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
    • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
    • It has been revealed that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a latest attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

    The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

    It has been revealed that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

    Recent findings suggest that “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

    This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

    “The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” mentioned Kondrashkin.

    In a recent development, the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

    Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

    On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

    #22046. Breaking: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (613 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
    • According to recent reports, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
    • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

    According to recent reports, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

    Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

    “My blueprint is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

    In a recent development, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

    Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

    Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

    Industry observers note that the Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

    Recent findings suggest that kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

    Kobusch aims to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line at the moment being attempted by a Russian team.

    This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

    Industry observers note that kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

    Recent findings suggest that simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his intends while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

    #22042. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1243 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
    • According to recent reports, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
    • Industry observers note that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It demonstrated again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

    According to recent reports, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

    Industry observers note that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

    After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang mentioned: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

    Industry observers note that several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

    Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

    Sources indicate that “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

    When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

    Recent findings suggest that during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

    On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

    According to recent reports, “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

    It has been revealed that in the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

    It has been revealed that “Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

    Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

    “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

    Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

    It has been revealed that “We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang stated. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

    Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

    The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

    The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

    Industry observers note that the climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

    Sources indicate that climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

    Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

    Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

    Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

    Recent findings suggest that on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

    Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he indicates:.

    Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

    It has been revealed that the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.
